verdict.reasoning: Low mood, low appetite, low energy, and weight loss are all described: “not having much of an appetite and energy lately,” “my mood's low,” and “have you lost any weight? – I have a little bit, yes.”

Symptoms are said to have been going on for months: “Started long, long ago… didn't really have energy,” and appetite loss for “Three months ago. Three and a half months ago,” with weight loss for “Something like that… six months.”

Appetite loss and stopping thyroxine began when he changed law firms, not 3–6 months after: “That must have started when I changed over to the new law firm… three and a half months ago” and “I have not been taking it… since I changed law firm.”
Weight loss amount and duration match: “roughly six months… how much have you lost? – …less than a stone. – So. About a stone? Yeah. Six months. Okay. Okay. Six kilos.”
He explicitly describes feeling down and out of place: “I’ve been feeling down… nothing is like feeling right. I feel out of place. And… just down.”
He reports headaches: “I have trouble at work sometimes. Having headaches, feeling nauseous.”
Nausea is repeatedly mentioned: “having headaches, feeling nauseous,” and “I feel nauseous every now and again… Not feeling very good. Trying to eat something but don't really want to.”

He notes palpitations and dyspnea particularly in a lift: “my heart starts beating and I can't really breathe,” and the clinician clarifies palpitations: “You’re… describing, like, palpitations to me… If you're feeling your own heartbeat. – Yeah.” Confined space (lift) is explicitly mentioned.
The clinician confirms walking tolerance: “So you can walk about a mile. And you don't feel short of breath at all? – That's right, yes.”
He reports very limited walking: “I haven't been walking lately at all… I haven't been feeling good enough or good at all.”
Work function described as okay: “I mean, work is okay. I have trouble at work sometimes… But I can do my work. That's okay.”
He denies chest pain: “Do you get any chest pains with it? – Not really, no… Patient: No chest pain.”

He denies diarrhea and vomiting, and bowels are okay: “your bowels. How's your toilet? – That's okay… you don't have any diarrhea? – No, no diarrhea? No.” and “You mentioned nausea. Have you been ever sick with it? – No, actually not.”
He denies cough: “You also mentioned that you're feeling short of breathing… Is there any cough? – No, not really. Just shortness of breath.”
Hematemesis and melena are never discussed; neither presence nor absence is mentioned in the transcript.
History of underactive thyroid is stated: “Yes. I had too little activity of my thyroid… Underactive thyroid? Yes.”
He previously took thyroxine: “And in that I took thyroxine.”
He stopped thyroxine since changing firms: “You're taking thyroxine. Are you using it every day? – Not anymore… I have not been taking it… since I changed law firm, I would say.”
It is clear thyroxine is a past, not current, medication: “I took thyroxine” (past) and “Not anymore… I have not been taking it in the last… since I changed law firm.”
He works as a lawyer and changed law firms: “Who likes to be a lawyer?” and “That must have started when I changed over to the new law firm.”
Other social history (e.g., smoking, alcohol, living situation) is not discussed; saying details are unclear correctly reflects missing information.

No vitals, exam findings, or lab results are recorded; only history and future plans are discussed. The clinician notes, “we would need to do a physical examination” and “I think a general set of bloods is a good idea,” implying they have not yet been done.

Low mood, appetite loss, low energy, and ~6 kg weight loss over ~6 months are documented, and the clinician explicitly considers systemic/thyroid causes: “underactive thyroid… I'm not quite clear on what picture we are having here… do a general set of bloods,” which is consistent with evaluating mood vs systemic/thyroid etiologies.

He has shortness of breath and palpitations mainly in the lift, but not exertional with walking: “Do you feel short of breath when you walk at all? – No, actually, no… So you can walk about a mile… – That's right, yes.” Thus “exertional dyspnea” is incorrect; it is situational (lift) rather than exertional.

There is hypothyroidism with nonadherence and concern it may contribute: “Underactive thyroid… I took thyroxine… Not anymore… since I changed law firm,” and the clinician plans bloods because “I'm not quite clear on what picture we are having here,” consistent with needing thyroid assessment and possible treatment decisions.

No recent labs or imaging are present, and a baseline lab evaluation is planned: “When was your last blood test? – Haven't taken one in a long time.” and “I think a general set of bloods is a good idea… where we look at things like anemia, how your kidney functions are, your livers, all that with vitamin levels.”

Blood tests are planned but specific panels (CBC, CMP, TSH, free T4, B12, folate, iron studies, vitamin D) are not itemized: the doctor only says “a general set of bloods… like anemia, how your kidney functions are, your livers, all that with vitamin levels,” without listing these exact tests.
Reassessing thyroid status and considering restarting thyroxine is not explicitly stated; only general blood tests are mentioned, with no explicit plan about TSH/free T4 or restarting thyroxine.

They plan coordination via support and SMS follow-up: “you need to ring up support so that we can organize that blood test for you… once you get the result, you will receive a text message through your phone to tell you to book an appointment.” The number is described as “an O300 number” in the app.
A physical exam after labs is planned: “If that's all clear, then we would need to do a physical examination… Then go in and do the thing.”

He is advised about chest pain and bowel changes but not syncope or severe shortness of breath: “with palpitations or chest pain… you need to go to A and E,” and “if your… bowels change or you're being sick again, you need to get in touch with us.” Syncope and severe SOB are not mentioned.
Follow-up after labs or earlier if unwell is discussed: “once you get the result… book an appointment… If you're feeling poorly, don't wait for that. Just get in touch with us again.”

Same as above: he is to have follow-up after labs, with earlier review if symptoms worsen: “book an appointment” after results and “If you're feeling poorly, don't wait for that. Just get in touch with us again.”
